# Homework: `data-*` Attributes & `dataset`

Five challenges, with short lessons in between. Each challenge should be its own HTML file (or folder) with plain JavaScript. No libraries.

Do them in order. Each lesson teaches what the challenges after it need.

---

## Lesson: What `data-*` Attributes Are

You can make up your own HTML attributes, as long as they start with `data-`:

```html
<button id="buy" data-product-id="42" data-price="9.99" data-in-stock>Buy</button>
```

The browser ignores them. They're for you: a place to attach extra information to an element.

Read and write them with `dataset`:

```js
const button = document.querySelector("#buy");

button.dataset.productId; // "42"
button.dataset.price;     // "9.99"
button.dataset.inStock;   // "" (it's there, but has no value)
button.dataset.color;     // undefined (it's not there)

button.dataset.color = "red";  // adds data-color="red" to the element
delete button.dataset.price;   // removes data-price from the element
```

Open the Elements tab in DevTools while you do this. You'll see the attributes appear and disappear in the HTML.

### The naming rule

The `data-` part is dropped, and the dashed name becomes camelCase:

| HTML attribute      | JavaScript            |
| ------------------- | --------------------- |
| `data-id`           | `dataset.id`          |
| `data-product-id`   | `dataset.productId`   |
| `data-is-very-long` | `dataset.isVeryLong`  |

It works in reverse too: `dataset.userName = "dug"` creates `data-user-name="dug"`.

Use lowercase and dashes in the HTML. `data-productId` in HTML does **not** become `dataset.productId` (HTML lowercases it to `data-productid`, which becomes `dataset.productid`).

## Challenge 1: Image Gallery

A big image at the top, a row of thumbnails underneath. Click a thumbnail to show it big.

**Requirements**

- At least 5 thumbnails. Each one is a small `<img>` with:
  - `data-full`: the URL of the big version
  - `data-caption`: a caption for it
- Clicking a thumbnail puts its `data-full` image in the big image, and shows its `data-caption` underneath.
- The currently selected thumbnail has a visible border. Only one at a time.
- Show "Image 3 of 5" somewhere. Give each thumbnail a `data-index` for this.

**Hints**

- Use event delegation: one click listener on the thumbnail row, then `event.target.dataset.full`.
- Clicking the gap between thumbnails gives you the row itself as `event.target`. Its `dataset.full` is `undefined`. Check for that and `return`.
- Free placeholder images: `https://picsum.photos/id/10/150/100` (small) and `https://picsum.photos/id/10/800/500` (big). Change the `10` for a different picture.

**Bonus**

- Previous / Next buttons that move through the images, wrapping around at the ends.

## Lesson: `dataset` Values Are Strings

Everything in `dataset` is a string, even if it looks like a number or a boolean:

```html
<div id="item" data-price="9.99" data-qty="2" data-done="false"></div>
```

```js
const item = document.querySelector("#item");

item.dataset.price + 1;          // "9.991"  ← string joining!
Number(item.dataset.price) + 1;  // 10.99

item.dataset.price * item.dataset.qty; // 19.98 (works by luck: * converts for you)
```

Booleans are worse:

```js
if (item.dataset.done) {
  // this runs! "false" is a non-empty string, so it's truthy
}

if (item.dataset.done === "true") {
  // this is what you meant
}
```

When you set a value, it's turned into a string too:

```js
item.dataset.qty = 3;          // data-qty="3"
item.dataset.tags = ["a", "b"]; // data-tags="a,b"
item.dataset.info = { a: 1 };  // data-info="[object Object]"  ← useless
```

### Checking if a data attribute exists

```js
"price" in item.dataset;  // true
"color" in item.dataset;  // false
```

This is better than `if (item.dataset.price)`, because an attribute with an empty value (`data-in-stock`) is `""`, and `""` is falsy.

### Finding elements by data attribute

`querySelector` can search by attribute:

```js
document.querySelector('[data-id="42"]');        // the element with that exact value
document.querySelectorAll("[data-in-stock]");    // every element that has it at all
document.querySelectorAll('[data-category="shoes"]');
```

## Challenge 2: Product Filter

A page of product cards that can be filtered and sorted. All the product info lives in `data-` attributes in the HTML.

**Requirements**

- At least 10 product cards written directly in the HTML, like this:

```html
<article class="product" data-category="shoes" data-price="59.99" data-rating="4.5" data-on-sale>
  <h3>Running Shoes</h3>
  <p>€59.99</p>
</article>
```

- Use at least 3 categories. Only some products have `data-on-sale`.
- Filter buttons at the top: "All" plus one per category. Each button has a `data-filter` attribute (`data-filter="shoes"`, `data-filter="all"`). One listener handles them all.
- A checkbox: "Only show items on sale".
- The category filter and the sale checkbox work **together**: "shoes that are on sale".
- A sort dropdown: price low to high, price high to low, best rated.
- Show "Showing 4 of 10 products", and keep it up to date.

**Hints**

- Hide cards with `card.hidden = true` / `false`.
- To sort DOM elements: get them into an array with `[...container.children]`, sort the array, then `container.append(...sortedCards)`. Appending an element that's already on the page **moves** it.
- Don't forget `Number()` when comparing prices. Try sorting `"9.99"` and `"59.99"` as strings and see what happens.
- Use `in` for the sale check, not truthiness. `data-on-sale` has no value, so `dataset.onSale` is `""`.

**Bonus**

- A "max price" range slider that also filters, working together with the other two filters.

## Lesson: Styling With Data Attributes

CSS can select elements by attribute, so data attributes are a great way to tell CSS what **state** something is in:

```css
[data-state="open"]   { background: lightyellow; }  /* exact value */
[data-state="closed"] { opacity: 0.5; }
[data-selected]       { outline: 2px solid blue; }  /* has the attribute at all */
```

Then JavaScript only changes the data attribute, and CSS handles the look:

```js
panel.dataset.state = panel.dataset.state === "open" ? "closed" : "open";

card.dataset.selected = "";     // turn on (attribute present)
delete card.dataset.selected;   // turn off (attribute gone)
```

Why not just classes? An element can only have **one** value for `data-state`. With classes, nothing stops an element from having both `open` and `closed` at the same time because you forgot to remove one.

### Putting the whole page in a state

Set a data attribute on `<html>` and every CSS rule on the page can react to it:

```css
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg: #111;
  --text: #eee;
}
body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
}
```

```js
document.documentElement.dataset.theme = "dark";
```

`document.documentElement` is the `<html>` element.

### Showing a data attribute's value with CSS

`attr()` puts an attribute's value into `content`:

```html
<span data-tooltip="This is a tooltip">Hover me</span>
```

```css
[data-tooltip]:hover::after {
  content: attr(data-tooltip);
}
```

## Challenge 3: Star Rating

Five stars. Hover to preview, click to choose.

**Requirements**

- Five star buttons (use ★ as the text), each with `data-value` from `1` to `5`.
- Lit-up stars have a `data-lit` attribute. Style them with `[data-lit]` in CSS. No classes.
- Hovering a star lights up that star and all the ones before it.
- Moving the mouse off the stars goes back to showing the chosen rating.
- Clicking sets the rating. Store it on the container: `data-rating="3"`.
- Show text below: "You rated this 3 out of 5", or "Not rated yet" if the container has no `data-rating`.
- A "Clear" button that removes `data-rating` from the container completely.
- Make **three** of these on the page, each working on its own. Write the code once, not three times.

**Hints**

- Write a function `setupRating(container)` and call it for each one: `document.querySelectorAll(".rating").forEach(setupRating)`.
- A function `showStars(container, n)` that lights up the first `n` stars is useful for hover, mouse-leave and click.
- Use `mouseover` on the container for hovering stars, and `mouseleave` on the container for leaving. (`mouseover` bubbles up from the stars, `mouseleave` doesn't fire when moving between stars.)
- Remember `dataset.value` is a string. Compare with `Number()`.

**Bonus**

- Each rating container has a `data-label` (like `data-label="Food"`). Under all three, show a summary: "Food: 4, Service: 2, Price: not rated".

## Challenge 4: Theme Switcher

Let the user pick a theme for the whole page.

**Requirements**

- At least 3 themes: light, dark, and one you make up.
- Buttons for each theme, with `data-theme-choice="dark"` etc. One listener handles them all.
- Clicking one sets `data-theme` on the `<html>` element.
- All colors in your CSS come from CSS variables, and each theme only changes the variables. No theme-specific rules for individual elements.
- The current theme's button has `data-active` and looks different (style it with `[data-active]`).
- Save the choice in `localStorage` and restore it when the page loads.

**Hints**

- Put a few things on the page so you can see the themes work: headings, paragraphs, a card, a button, a link.
- If there's nothing saved yet, use `window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches` to pick light or dark based on the user's system.
- To find the button for the current theme: ``document.querySelector(`[data-theme-choice="${theme}"]`)``.

**Bonus**

- A font size setting done the same way: `data-font-size="small" | "medium" | "large"` on `<html>`, saved separately.

## Lesson: `data-action` and `data-id`

### `data-action`

When there are lots of buttons that do different things, describe **what each button does** in the HTML, and have one listener decide:

```html
<div id="counter">
  <button data-action="decrement">-</button>
  <span id="count">0</span>
  <button data-action="increment">+</button>
  <button data-action="reset">Reset</button>
</div>
```

```js
let count = 0;

document.querySelector("#counter").addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest("[data-action]");
  if (!button) return;

  const action = button.dataset.action;
  if (action === "increment") count++;
  if (action === "decrement") count--;
  if (action === "reset") count = 0;

  document.querySelector("#count").textContent = count;
});
```

Why `closest()` instead of `event.target`? If the button has an icon or `<span>` inside it, `event.target` is the span. `closest("[data-action]")` walks up until it finds the element with the attribute.

### `data-id`: point at your data, don't store it

Data attributes are good for **pointing at** your data. They're not a good place to **keep** your data.

```html
<!-- Good: the DOM says which item this is -->
<li data-id="42">Milk</li>

<!-- Avoid: now your data lives in HTML strings -->
<li data-item='{"id":42,"name":"Milk","qty":2,"price":1.2}'>Milk</li>
```

Keep the real data in a JavaScript array or object, draw the page from it, and use `data-id` to find the right entry when something is clicked:

```js
let items = [
  { id: "42", name: "Milk", qty: 2 },
  { id: "43", name: "Bread", qty: 1 },
];

list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest("[data-action]");
  if (!button) return;

  const id = button.closest("[data-id]").dataset.id;
  const item = items.find((item) => item.id === id);

  if (button.dataset.action === "more") item.qty++;
  if (button.dataset.action === "remove") items = items.filter((i) => i.id !== id);

  render();
});
```

The rule of thumb: **the array is the truth, the data attributes are labels.**

## Challenge 5: Cinema Seat Booking

Bigger one, uses everything. Plan before you code.

**The room**

- Generate the seats with JavaScript, don't write them by hand: 8 rows (A–H), 10 seats per row.
- Each seat is a `<button>` with:
  - `data-seat="C7"` (row + number)
  - `data-row="C"`
  - `data-status="available" | "taken" | "selected"`
  - `data-vip` (only on rows G and H)
- Some seats are already taken when the page loads. Put their IDs in an array, like `["A3", "A4", "D7", "F1"]`.

**Requirements**

1. Style seats **only** through data attribute selectors: `[data-status="taken"]`, `[data-status="selected"]`, `[data-vip]`. No classes for state.
2. Clicking an available seat selects it. Clicking a selected seat unselects it. Clicking a taken seat does nothing.
3. Normal seats cost €9, VIP seats €14. Show a summary that updates live: which seats are selected ("C7, C8, G2") and the total price.
4. Maximum 6 seats per booking.
5. Below the seats, two buttons: `data-action="book"` and `data-action="clear"`. Book turns all selected seats into taken seats. Clear unselects everything.
6. Save taken seats to `localStorage` so bookings survive a refresh.

**Rules**

- One click listener for the whole page (or one for the seat grid and one for the buttons, at most).
- Keep the taken and selected seats in arrays (or a `Set`). The `data-status` attributes **display** the state, they aren't the state. Never read `data-status` to decide anything.
- A `render()` function that loops over every seat and sets its `data-status` from your arrays. Call it after every change.

**Hints**

- `String.fromCharCode(65 + i)` gives you `"A"`, `"B"`, `"C"`... for `i = 0, 1, 2...`
- Is a seat VIP? You can check `"vip" in seat.dataset`, or work it out from the row in your data. Pick one and be consistent.

**Bonus**

- A row of "price legend" items at the top (`[data-vip]` seat, normal seat, taken seat) that reuse the exact same CSS as the real seats.

**Extra hard bonus**

- Selected seats must be next to each other in the same row. If the user clicks a seat that isn't next to their current selection, either refuse it (with a message) or start a new selection from that seat. Your choice, but explain it on the page.
